lessons.body:
Module 4 is **Case 2**. You keep the 200-transaction retail CSV from Case 1, but the task changes: instead of drawing charts, you investigate one region, compare options and plan a next step for a manager. Everything you need is attached to this lesson.

## The files

| File | What it holds | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **Lecture notes** (PDF, whole course) | Period 10 sections 10.1 to 10.5, Period 11 sections 11.1 to 11.4, Period 12 sections 12.1 to 12.7, each with worked prompts, checked tables, key concepts and review questions | The full wording of each prompt and every table of figures |
| **Slides, 150 pages** (PDF) | The complete deck. Each period has a checkpoint question and a key-takeaways slide; Periods 10 and 11 also have a "Review the prompts" slide | Following the prompt sequence slide by slide |
| **Slides, 81 pages** (PDF) | A short version of the same deck. It keeps the main prompt slides and drops the dividers, review slides, checkpoints and takeaways | A quick preview or revision |
| **Activity 3 sheet, Student version** (PDF) | "Evidence-Based Retail Decision Making": a guided workflow, evidence ledger, option matrix, handover checklist and a practice rubric. About 100 to 130 minutes | The hands-on task. It is also set as the assignment of Period 12 |
| **Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv** | 200 transactions, 13 columns | Recalculating every figure yourself |

## Where each period is

| Period | Lecture notes | 150-page slides | 81-page slides |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 Diagnose with Data (Case 2) | 10.1 to 10.5 | 99 to 108 | 54 to 59 |
| 11 Develop Evidence-Based Options | 11.1 to 11.4 | 109 to 116 | 60 only |
| 12 Plan and Measure Action | 12.1 to 12.7 | 117 to 127 | 61 to 65 |

> [!meo] The short deck keeps only one Period 11 slide (Generate Options). The comparison, challenge and choice steps are on slides 111 to 113 of the 150-page deck, so use that deck, or the lesson, for them.

## What the CSV can and cannot tell you

The file has thirteen columns: `Transaction_ID`, `Store_Region` (East, North, South, West), `Product_Category` (Apparel, Electronics, Furniture, Grocery), `Payment_Method`, `Customer_Type`, `Unit_Price`, `Items_Sold`, `Gross_Amount`, `Discount_Percent`, `Discount_Amount`, `Net_Sales_Amount`, `Average_Price_Per_Item` and `Effective_Discount_Per_Item`.

It has **no** transaction dates, store identifiers or store counts, operating days, currency, targets, costs, profit or campaign results. Throughout Module 4 you will meet claims that need one of these. The right response is to name the missing input, not to guess it.

## How to study this module

1. **Open the CSV in a spreadsheet** and keep it open. Every table of figures in the lessons can be reproduced with a pivot table or `COUNTIFS` and `SUMIFS`.
2. **Read a period lesson**, trying each "Predict before you read" and "Find the error" box before you open it.
3. **Do the quiz** with a confidence rating for each answer. Questions that need a calculation are marked as work-on-paper: do them in the spreadsheet first.
4. **Open the matching lecture notes sections** for the full worked prompts, and use the slides as a checklist of the prompt sequence.
5. **After Period 12, do Activity 3.** Its first four stages follow Periods 10 to 12. Its handover folder uses the documentation habits you meet in Periods 13 and 14, so you may finish that part after Module 5.

> [!ghi-nho] Do not upload customer names, phone numbers, employee data or private business exports to a chatbot. The practice CSV contains none of these, and the Activity 3 sheet asks you to keep it that way.

lessons.title: Period 10 · Diagnose with Data — Case 2
lessons.description: Case 2 begins. Frame a constrained investigation, build and check a regional overview, drill into East by product category, and write a working diagnosis that separates verified facts from hypotheses.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Write a task brief for a constrained business investigation: audience, input, decision, outputs and success criteria
Build a regional overview of transaction count, total net sales and net sales per transaction, and reconcile it to the 200-row CSV
Explain why a low regional total can come from fewer records, a lower value per record, or both
Break one region down by product category and check that the categories add back to the region
Sort claims into verified finding, working hypothesis, missing input and decision to defer
Write a two-sentence diagnosis that contains one verified fact and one clearly labelled hypothesis
lessons.body:
A retail manager has time to investigate **one** region. In Case 1 you drew the regional bar chart, and one bar was clearly the shortest: East. Now the manager asks, "Why is East low, and what should we do about it?"

This period answers only the first half of that question, and answers it honestly. You will check the numbers, find out *what kind* of low East is, and stop at the edge of what the file can tell you.

> [!ghi-nho] A total is **count × average value**. A low total can mean few records, small records, or both. Find out which one before anyone proposes a fix.

:::Predict before you read
East has the smallest total net sales of the four regions. Before you look at any table, write down which you expect: (a) East has the fewest transactions, (b) East has the lowest net sales per transaction, or (c) both. Add one line of reasoning. You will check your prediction in the section "Explore: build and check the overview".
:::

parts.md:
The CSV holds transaction records and nothing else about the business. So the first job is not "fix East". It is to **find a pattern worth investigating** and to say what extra evidence you would need. Asking for a promotion strategy or a sales forecast at this point would be premature.

Write a task brief before the first analysis prompt:

| Element | Case 2 |
|---|---|
| Audience | The retailer's manager |
| Input | The 200-row CSV |
| Decision | What to investigate first, before committing resources |
| Outputs | Regional evidence table, East category breakdown, supported diagnosis, alternative explanations, missing-data request |
| Success | Correct totals, explicit limitations, a defensible pause before any intervention |

```prompt Clarification prompt (use before analysing)
Before analysing, ask me what one decision the manager needs to make, what data are available and what output will help. Ask only questions that could change the task. Then draft a four-part brief for my confirmation.
```

**Why it works:** it makes the AI ask about the decision before it touches the data, and the limit ("only questions that could change the task") stops it from interrogating you. You still confirm the brief, so the task stays yours.

Now compare two ways of asking for the first analysis.

```prompt Prompt A — weak
Why is East doing badly? Tell me how to fix it.
```

**Why it is weak:** "badly" is assumed, not shown. "Why" asks for a cause the file cannot give. "Fix it" asks for an action before any figure has been checked. No calculation rule is named, so nobody could verify the answer.

```prompt Prompt B — regional overview
Use the supplied CSV to show each Store_Region's transaction count, SUM(Net_Sales_Amount), and net sales per transaction (regional sum divided by count). Sort by total recorded net sales. Include an all-region total, state the calculation rule, and identify one surprising pattern to examine. Do not recommend an intervention yet.
```

**Why it is better:** it names the fields and the formula, fixes the sort order, asks for an all-region total you can reconcile, and holds recommendations back.

> [!meo] Use an AI chatbot with file-analysis capability if you have one. If yours cannot analyse files, build the tables in a spreadsheet, paste the *verified* tables into the chat with a source label, and ask the AI to help with the diagnosis. Record what each tool actually did.

sections.title: Explore: build and check the overview

parts.md:
Here is the regional overview, recalculated from all 200 rows of the CSV.

| Store region | Transactions | Total net sales | Net sales per transaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| North | 57 | 260,026.33 | 4,561.87 |
| South | 53 | 236,980.99 | 4,471.34 |
| West | 51 | 213,240.41 | 4,181.18 |
| East | 39 | 182,004.38 | 4,666.78 |
| **All regions** | **200** | **892,252.11** | **4,461.26** |

Net sales per transaction is each group's sum divided by **its own** record count. For East: 182,004.38 / 39 = 4,666.78. The all-region figure is 892,252.11 / 200.

> [!canh-bao] The all-region average, 4,461.26, is **not** the plain average of the four regional averages. That unweighted average is 4,470.29, which is wrong because North has 57 records and East only 39. Divide the total by the total count.

**Verified finding.** East has the smallest total and the fewest recorded transactions, yet the highest net sales per recorded transaction. So its low total is associated with fewer records, not with an unusually low value per record. The evidence does not say *why* fewer records were captured, and a small count alone does not establish weak demand.

Now check your prediction. Only (a) is right. East is lowest on count but **highest** on value per transaction, so (b) and (c) are wrong.

> [!vi-du] Currency is not stated in the file, so the figures above have no currency symbol. If an AI answer adds a dollar or dong sign, treat that as invented.

sections.title: Two measures, two different stories
sections.intro: Total net sales = transactions × net sales per transaction. Split East's low total into its two parts and compare each with the other regions.

parts.title: How many records (count)
parts.md:
- East: **39**, the fewest
- North 57, South 53, West 51
- East holds **19.5%** of the 200 records
- Fewer records pull East's total down
- Possible reasons are untested: fewer stores in the extract, a shorter reporting window, or really fewer purchases

parts.title: How much per record (value)
parts.md:
- East: **4,666.78**, the highest
- North 4,561.87, South 4,471.34, West 4,181.18
- East holds **20.4%** of net sales, a little more than its share of records
- Value per record does not explain East's low total; it works the other way
- Value is a mean, so a few large sales can move it

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] Show count and value on **separate** charts. They are different measures with different scales, and one unlabelled axis hides the difference.

parts.md:
Compare recorded counts and per-transaction values using two clearly labelled charts. For a beginner, two small bar charts are easier to read than a dual-axis chart.

```prompt Follow-up — explain the pattern
Make separate bar charts for transaction counts and net sales per transaction. Use the verified regional table. Explain how the two measures differ. State one supported observation about East and two explanations we cannot test with these fields.
```

**Why it works:** it reuses the table you already checked instead of asking for a fresh calculation, and it forces the AI to separate what is observed from what is only possible.

A defensible reading is: East has 39 records and 4,666.78 net sales per transaction. Candidate reasons for the count difference include a different number of stores, a shorter observation window, or genuine differences in purchase activity. **All three remain untested.** A difference in counts can motivate a follow-up question; it does not establish demand or reporting coverage.

sections.title: Break down the results: East by category

parts.md:
To see where East's records are concentrated, filter to East and group by `Product_Category`.

```prompt Follow-up — East category breakdown
Filter Store_Region to East and group by Product_Category. Return transaction counts, total net sales and net sales per transaction for each category. Show full values and reconcile the categories with East's 39 transactions and 182,004.38 total net sales. Identify the category with the fewest records.
```

| East product category | Transactions | Net sales | Net sales per transaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apparel | 12 | 60,036.03 | 5,003.00 |
| Electronics | 4 | 10,559.24 | 2,639.81 |
| Furniture | 10 | 59,183.24 | 5,918.32 |
| Grocery | 13 | 52,225.87 | 4,017.37 |
| **East total** | **39** | **182,004.38** | **4,666.78** |

**Reconcile first.** 12 + 4 + 10 + 13 = 39, and the four category totals add to 182,004.38. If your own table does not reconcile, stop and find the cause before reading any further into it.

Electronics has the fewest records, only four. That makes it a **candidate investigation point**, not evidence that the Electronics business failed. Four rows is a small subgroup: one large or small sale moves its average a lot, and the result can depend on which stores or periods the extract happens to include.

> [!canh-bao] A segment that looks odd is a question to ask, not a finding to announce. "Electronics has 4 records" is a fact. "East has an Electronics problem" is a hypothesis that needs more evidence.

sections.title: Form a working diagnosis: the claim register
sections.intro: Keep different levels of certainty apart. A claim register gives every statement one of five labels and says what supports it.

parts.title: Verified finding
parts.md:
*East has 39 records and 182,004.38 net sales.*

Supported by: grouped CSV calculations.

parts.title: Verified comparison
parts.md:
*East has the highest net sales per recorded transaction.*

Supported by: regional ratios checked from the CSV.

parts.title: Working hypothesis
parts.md:
*East may have fewer active stores or a shorter reporting window.*

Plausible, but **not tested** by the CSV.

parts.title: Missing input
parts.md:
*Store identifiers, extraction dates, store opening days.*

Needed to assess comparable activity.

parts.title: Decision to defer
parts.md:
*Do not choose a promotion solely from regional totals.*

Cause and exposure are unknown.

sections.outro:
```prompt Synthesis prompt
Combine the regional overview and East category table. Write two checked findings, one cautious working diagnosis, and two alternative explanations. Label the alternatives as hypotheses. End with the most useful question for the data owner. Do not imply that a hypothesis has been confirmed.
```

**Why it works:** the labels in the prompt become labels in the answer, so you can scan for a hypothesis dressed as a finding.

The next sensible question is whether the **same stores and time windows** were represented in all four regions. That decides whether a fair comparison of transaction activity is possible at all. The CSV contains no store identifiers, transaction dates, profit or currency, and none of them should be made up.

parts.title: Why not ask the AI straight away for the cause of East's low total?
parts.md: Because the file cannot contain a cause. It holds what was recorded, not why. An AI will still produce a confident-sounding cause if you ask for one, so ask for observations, alternatives and the data that would separate them.

parts.title: Is East underperforming?
parts.md: Not on the evidence you have. East is lowest on total and count and highest on value per record. "Underperforming" needs a target or a fair baseline, such as transactions per active store per operating day, and the file provides neither.

parts.title: Is the highest value per record just a few big sales?
parts.md: Worth checking. Individual transactions range from 77.30 to 16,008.39, so a mean can be pulled by large sales. East also has the highest **median** net sales per transaction (4,272.72, against 3,613.42 for North, 2,899.77 for West and 2,742.34 for South), so the reading does not depend on a handful of sales. Checking a second statistic is a good habit.

parts.title: The chatbot gave a total that does not match mine. Which do I use?
parts.md: The file is the benchmark. Recompute with a pivot table, find where the two differ (a missing region, a rounded figure, a different filter) and reconcile before you go on. Never adjust a regional figure to make a total fit.

Reproduce these figures in a spreadsheet before the quiz.

1. Insert a pivot table on the full CSV: rows `Store_Region`, values **Count of Transaction_ID** and **Sum of Net_Sales_Amount**. Divide each sum by its count at full precision and round only for display.
2. Confirm that the four counts add to 200, the four sums add to 892,252.11, and the count of unique `Transaction_ID` values is 200 (it should equal the row count).
3. Filter to East, pivot on `Product_Category`, and confirm that the category counts add to 39 and the totals to 182,004.38.
4. Optional: compute the median of `Net_Sales_Amount` for each region and see whether East is still highest.

:::Find the error
An AI summary says: "East is our weakest region: only 182,004.38 in net sales from 39 transactions, about 4,667 per transaction. East customers clearly spend less, so weak demand is the cause and a promotion will lift East immediately."

Find at least three problems before you open this box.
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
1. "Weakest" rests on the total alone. East's 4,667 per transaction is the **highest** of the four regions, so "customers spend less" contradicts the figures the summary itself quotes.
2. "Weak demand is the cause" is a hypothesis. The file has no store, date or traffic data, so fewer stores or a shorter reporting window fit the same numbers.
3. "A promotion will lift East immediately" is a forecast. The CSV contains no experiment, cost or campaign result that could support it.
:::

A small or odd segment worth a closer look, not evidence of a failure or a cause.
Which stores, entities and time periods a data extract includes. Unequal coverage can make counts incomparable.

questions.prompt: What is the first numerical overview used in the retail diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The CSV records net sales by region and category, so a regional total of Net_Sales_Amount is the first overview you can build and check. Customer lifetime value, monthly profit by store and campaign return all need fields the file does not have (customer history, costs, dates, store IDs, campaign data).

Monthly profit by store
Net sales totals by region
Campaign return on investment

questions.prompt: A manager asks which region should receive an initial review based on total net sales. Which is the lowest?
questions.explanation: East's total is 182,004.38, below West (213,240.41), South (236,980.99) and North (260,026.33). The ranking is a verified fact, but it does not say why East is lowest. North is the highest, not the lowest, a common slip when a table is read in the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: What does a transaction count represent in this dataset?
questions.explanation: Each row is one transaction, so the count is the number of recorded transactions. The file has no store ID, date or customer ID, so stores, operating days and repeat customers cannot be inferred from the row count.

options.label: The number of recorded transactions
The number of operating business days
The number of unique store locations
The number of repeat customers

questions.prompt: East records fewer transactions but high net sales per transaction. Which interpretation is safest?
questions.explanation: A total is count times average value, so East's low total and high value per transaction together show that the total reflects both. "Fewer stores" is a plausible hypothesis but stores are not in the file, and margin and purchasing power would need cost and customer data.

options.label: The region has the smallest profit margin
The region has the weakest purchasing power
The region operates with fewer stores
The observed totals reflect both count and value

questions.prompt: Which CSV field identifies the retail product group?
questions.explanation: Product_Category defines Apparel, Electronics, Furniture and Grocery. Transaction_ID identifies a record, Customer_Type describes the buyer type and Payment_Method records how the sale was paid, so none of them groups products.

Transaction_ID
Customer_Type

questions.prompt: A student wants to investigate East's category mix. Which grouping should be used?
questions.explanation: Store_Region and Product_Category are both in the file, so East records grouped by Product_Category is a breakdown you can build. The CSV has no month, store ID or profit field, so the other groupings cannot be calculated from it.

options.label: All records grouped by estimated profit
East records grouped by transaction month
All records grouped by unknown store IDs
East records grouped by Product_Category

questions.prompt: Regional net-sales sums total 892,252.11. An AI summary reports 890,000.00. What is best?
questions.explanation: The sum from the file, 892,252.11, is the benchmark. The AI figure is 2,252.11 lower, so recompute from the file and find the difference. Bending a regional figure, calling the gap a loss, or using a rounded number unchecked all skip that reconciliation.

questions.prompt: East has the fewest recorded transactions. What is a defensible first management question?
questions.explanation: Fewer recorded transactions could reflect fewer stores, a shorter extraction window or lower activity, and the file cannot tell them apart. The defensible first question is whether store and time coverage are comparable, before anyone sets targets, closes stores or blames a promotion.

Should all East stores be closed now?

The file does contain discount fields, so "discount amounts are absent" is false, but their presence does not prove the claim.

Discount amounts are absent from the CSV
All regions have identical net sales

questions.prompt: What is net sales per transaction calculated as?
questions.explanation: Net sales per transaction is the total net sales of a group divided by that group's own transaction count: for East, 182,004.38 / 39 = 4,666.78. The other ratios (discount shares, units per transaction) answer different questions.

Choose whichever explanation sounds stronger

A proven causal model of demand

questions.explanation: Counts and totals checked in the CSV are verified findings. A plausible explanation the file cannot test is a working hypothesis. The fields you would need to test it are missing inputs. A choice you postpone until evidence exists is a decision to defer.

lessons.title: Period 11 · Develop Evidence-Based Options
lessons.description: Turn the East diagnosis into three investigative options, compare them on evidence and assumptions, challenge an attractive promotion idea and record a human choice.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Ask AI for three next-step options that each state the evidence they respond to, an unconfirmed assumption and the new information required
Compare options in a four-column table and judge which new data would most change the decision
Challenge an unsupported promotion proposal by naming two alternative explanations and a check for each
Explain why historical discount values in the CSV do not establish the effect of a future promotion
Record a human-approved direction with a justification and the findings that would change it
Check an AI option table against five questions before using it
lessons.body:
On Monday the manager reads your East diagnosis and says: "Good. Let's run a discount promotion in East next week." It sounds decisive, and an AI assistant will happily write the campaign.

Stop and list what you actually know. East has 39 recorded transactions, the fewest, and the highest net sales per transaction. The file has no store list, no dates, no costs and no campaign history. Nothing in it says *why* East has fewer records, or that a discount would change that.

> [!ghi-nho] At this stage ask AI for **next steps for investigation**, not for actions that spend money. A good option list shows what you would need to know in order to choose safely.

:::Predict before you read
The manager proposes a discount promotion for East. List two things, other than weak customer demand, that could explain East's low record count. Then write one check that could tell each of them apart from weak demand. You will compare your list with the challenge section.
:::

parts.md:
Ask for investigative options and make the AI expose what each one rests on.

```prompt Prompt A — weak
What should we do to boost East sales?
```

**Why it is weak:** it assumes East needs a boost, asks for actions instead of investigations, and does not ask the AI to show evidence, assumptions or data needs. The answer will sound actionable and be impossible to check.

```prompt Prompt B — option generation
Using the verified East diagnosis, suggest three useful next steps. For each, state the observed evidence it responds to, an unconfirmed assumption, and new information required. Include at least one data-coverage check. Keep sales interventions conditional on additional evidence.
```

**Why it is better:** the three fields it demands (evidence, assumption, new information) turn each option into something you can test, and the coverage check keeps the most basic question on the list.

A suitable answer would suggest checking reporting coverage, comparing store-level activity and investigating customer acquisition **only if** a meaningful activity shortfall remains after that. These are proposed approaches, not results of any business experiment.

Put the options side by side so their evidence and assumptions are visible before you choose.

```prompt Follow-up — comparison table
Put these options in a comparison table: option, current evidence, assumption to test, and information needed. Keep each entry brief; treat assumptions as unconfirmed.
```

| Option | Current evidence | Assumption to test | Information needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Check source coverage | East has 39 records, the fewest | Source includes unequal periods or stores | Store list, dates, extraction rules |
| Compare activity on a common basis | East's net sales per record is comparatively high | Stores may differ in activity | Store IDs, opening days, customer visits |
| Investigate acquisition | East has fewer recorded transactions | Customer demand may be weaker | Traffic or visits, conversion, campaign costs |

Every option has different prerequisites:

- **Source-coverage check.** Conceptually simple, and it protects every later analysis.
- **Common-basis comparison.** Needs a fair denominator, such as transactions per active store per operating day, *if* the organisation can supply and validate those fields.
- **Acquisition analysis.** Needs evidence of demand, the costs, and a proper evaluation design before any claim about performance.

Two test questions help you choose when only one check can be funded this week. Would the extra data **materially change the decision**? And what is the **information value relative to the effort**? An option that sounds impressive but cannot change what you do is a poor first choice.

> [!canh-bao] The table must label assumptions as assumptions. If the "Assumption" column reads like a finding ("East demand is weaker"), the AI has smuggled a hypothesis in as evidence.

sections.title: Challenge an option
sections.intro: An AI may suggest: *"Run a discount promotion in East to increase purchases."* It is attractive because it sounds like action. A good reviewer asks what else could explain the problem and what is missing.

parts.title: Why the idea is attractive
parts.md:
- It is concrete and quick to explain
- East has the fewest records, so "more purchases" seems the obvious goal
- The CSV even contains discount columns, so it feels data-backed

parts.title: What the file does not contain
parts.md:
- Store identifiers and reporting dates, so coverage is unknown
- Costs, gross margin or profit
- Any experiment or campaign result
- Customer visits or traffic

Discounts are recorded only as past values on each transaction. They cannot show what a future promotion would do.

sections.outro:
```prompt Challenge prompt
Challenge the proposal to run a promotion in East. Identify two alternative reasons for its smaller recorded transaction count. For each, state a check that could distinguish it from lower customer demand. Explain which facts must be established before we spend on a promotion.
```

**Why it works:** it asks for alternatives *and* a way to tell them apart, so the answer is a to-do list rather than an opinion.

Two basic alternatives are **fewer stores represented in the extract** and **a shorter reporting period**. Checking store and time coverage is a prerequisite for any comparison. Even if East's count stays low after adjusting for coverage, customer traffic, pricing, product availability and competing conditions may matter. Do not say any of them is responsible until it has been measured.

If you listed fewer stores, a shorter window or a different traffic level in the "Predict" box, you were on the right lines. Each of those has a check: the store list, the extraction dates, the visit counts.

> [!vi-du] The CSV does show that East's overall discount rate (total `Discount_Amount` divided by total `Gross_Amount`) is 12.45%, the lowest of the four regions (North 13.32%, South 14.28%, West 15.97%). Someone could tell a story from that: "East discounts least, so fewer people buy." It is only a story. The file has no experiment, so it fits equally well with discounts being irrelevant to the count.

sections.title: Select a direction: the human decision gate
sections.intro: The AI may recommend, but a person chooses. The teaching example chooses **verify coverage first**. This is a human decision based on missing source information and the risk of misreading transaction counts. It is not proof that East has a coverage error.

parts.title: State the choice
parts.md: Name one direction in plain words: *check regional store and reporting coverage before any campaign.*

parts.title: Justify it with verified evidence
parts.md:
```prompt Human-approved choice prompt
We choose to check regional store and reporting coverage before any campaign. Write a two-sentence justification using the verified East evidence. Then identify what outcome from the coverage check would justify a deeper sales investigation. Do not claim that the coverage problem has already been found.
```

A useful justification: *East has fewer recorded transactions while having the highest recorded net sales per transaction. Without comparable store and reporting-period coverage, these counts do not establish a demand problem.*

parts.title: Say what would change the choice
parts.md: For example: if the coverage check shows the same stores and the same period in every region, the low count is more likely to be real activity, and a deeper look at demand becomes justified.

parts.title: Record the decision
parts.md:
| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Direction chosen | Check coverage first |
| Chosen by | The manager or named decision owner |
| Evidence used | East: 39 records, 4,666.78 per transaction |
| Assumptions | Coverage may differ between regions |
| Deferred options | Promotion; acquisition analysis |
| What would change it | Matching coverage with the count still low |

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] The value of this choice is that the next analysis will be better specified. Save the options and challenge record, so a later reviewer can see why the promotion was deferred.

sections.title: Check the recommendation before use
sections.intro: Before you accept an AI option table, ask these five questions.

parts.title: 1. Traceable?
parts.md: Is every stated number or observation traceable to the CSV and a calculation you have seen?

parts.title: 2. Assumptions labelled?
parts.md: Does the table mark assumptions as assumptions, not as findings?

parts.title: 3. Requests necessary?
parts.md: Is each new data request needed to choose between the options?

parts.title: 4. Feasible follow-up?
parts.md: Does the proposal give a follow-up you can actually do, rather than an unsupported causal conclusion?

parts.title: 5. A person chose?
parts.md: Has a named person, not the chatbot, picked the next step?

parts.title: Is a coverage check just a way of delaying?
parts.md: No. It is cheap, it protects every later analysis, and it can change the decision. If East's low count turns out to be a coverage artefact, a promotion would have treated a data problem as a business problem.

parts.title: Can the AI choose between the options?
parts.md: It can rank and justify them, which is useful input. The choice, and the accountability for it, stays with the manager or designated decision owner.

parts.title: Two options cite the same East total but recommend opposite actions. How do I decide?
parts.md: Compare their assumptions and the evidence for each. Shared descriptive data can support different hypotheses, so the assumptions decide whether an action is justified. Do not average the two actions or pick the one that sounds more confident.

parts.title: What if an option needs data we do not have, such as customer visits?
parts.md: Keep it on the list as **contingent on new evidence**. You cannot estimate visits from transaction IDs, and you should not report the effect as proven.

1. In the spreadsheet, compute each region's discount rate as the sum of `Discount_Amount` divided by the sum of `Gross_Amount`. You should get East 12.45%, North 13.32%, South 14.28% and West 15.97%. Then write one sentence about what this does **not** show.
2. Take an AI-written option table and, for every number in it, find the cell or pivot that supports it. Any number you cannot trace is unverified.
3. Write two questions that would test whether East's 39 transactions are comparable to another region's count.

:::Find the error
An AI option list says: "Option 1: run a 15% discount in East. East customers respond poorly to current pricing, and this will raise transactions by about 12% within a month. Information needed: none, the CSV is sufficient."

Find at least three problems before you open this box.
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
1. "East customers respond poorly to current pricing" is an unlabelled assumption. Nothing in the CSV measures how customers respond to price.
2. "Raise transactions by about 12% within a month" is an invented forecast. There is no experiment, baseline or timing in the file.
3. "Information needed: none" is false. A promotion needs coverage, cost and demand evidence, and an evaluation design, none of which the CSV holds.
:::

items.meaning: A candidate course of action or investigation. At this stage, prefer investigations that expose what you would need to know.
A statement used for planning that has not been established. An option table must label assumptions as assumptions.
items.example: Customer demand may be weaker in East.

items.meaning: Another plausible account of the same observation.
items.example: East's smaller count could reflect fewer stores or a shorter reporting period.

items.meaning: Missing information that limits a conclusion, such as store IDs, dates or customer visits.
Option, current evidence, assumption to test and information needed, kept brief so differences are visible.
The best criterion when only one check can be funded: how much the answer would change the decision, against how hard it is to get.
A prompt that asks for alternative explanations and a check to tell them apart, to expose assumptions rather than to add certainty.
An explicit human approval before moving from options to action.
An option that depends on evidence you do not yet hold, so it stays a hypothesis to investigate.

summary: Produce options only after the evidence is understood, and ask for next investigative steps with their evidence, assumptions and information needed.
Compare options in a table where assumptions are labelled, then challenge the most attractive one: historical discount values cannot show what a future promotion would do.
A person chooses the direction and records why. In the East example, verifying store and reporting coverage comes first.
Check every AI option table for traceable numbers, labelled assumptions, necessary data requests, a feasible follow-up and a human choice.

questions.prompt: After diagnosing East's recorded sales, what should AI help generate?
questions.explanation: After a diagnosis, AI's job is to propose next investigation steps and what each would need. It cannot supply past dates the file lacks, guarantee a campaign result or approve spending; spending needs a person's approval.

options.label: Unverified historical dates
Next investigation options
Automatic expenditure approvals
Guaranteed campaign results

questions.prompt: East appears to have low recorded activity. Which next step addresses comparability?
questions.explanation: Store counts and reporting coverage test directly whether East's recorded count is comparable with the other regions. Assuming equal stores, concluding that East has fewer customers, or raising prices all act on an explanation that has not been checked.

options.label: Check store counts and reporting coverage
Assume the sample contains equal stores
Conclude the region has fewer customers
Increase prices before gathering evidence

questions.prompt: What should an options comparison make explicit?
questions.explanation: A comparison is useful when it shows what evidence each option needs, so you can see which ones can be tested now. Prompt length, colour preferences and the chatbot's writing style say nothing about the quality of an option.

options.label: Evidence needed for each option
The length of the generated prompt
The manager's preferred slide colors
The chatbot's favorite writing style

questions.prompt: A manager can fund only one diagnostic check this week. Which criterion best guides selection?
questions.explanation: With one check to fund, choose the one whose answer would change the decision most for the effort it takes. Enthusiasm, length and the number of tool names are presentation, not value.

options.label: How enthusiastic the AI sounds
Which option has the longest description
Information value relative to effort
Which option uses the most tool names

questions.prompt: AI suggests a discount campaign because East has low total sales. What challenge is most pertinent?
questions.explanation: The suggestion assumes discounts are linked to East's low total, and the CSV has no experiment or cost data to show that, so ask what evidence links them. Stronger wording or another chart colour changes presentation only, and a made-up baseline would be invented.

options.label: Can the recommendation use stronger adjectives?
Can the manager add a fictional baseline?
What evidence links discounts to the problem?
Would another chart color improve the claim?

questions.prompt: Three options each require different new inputs. What should the comparison table include?
questions.explanation: A comparison table should show the data each option needs, what it is likely to be worth and the effort it takes. Guaranteed financial effects cannot be known from this file, and headlines or popularity do not support a reasoned choice.

options.label: Guaranteed financial effects for each
Only a persuasive headline per option
Required data, likely value and effort
Only estimated popularity and font style

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of challenging an AI-proposed option?
questions.explanation: Challenge makes hidden assumptions visible and shows what evidence is missing. It does not make a recommendation more certain, change the business question or throw away totals you have already verified.

options.label: Make every recommendation more certain
Replace the business question entirely
Discard all independently checked totals
Reveal assumptions and missing evidence

questions.prompt: One option seems attractive but needs customer visit data unavailable today. What is most defensible?
questions.explanation: An option that needs unavailable visit data stays a hypothesis, contingent on obtaining that data. Calling the effect proven or the gap irrelevant ignores the gap, and visits cannot be estimated from transaction IDs.

options.label: Report the visitor effect as proven
Treat the data gap as irrelevant
Estimate visits from transaction IDs
Describe it as contingent on new evidence

questions.prompt: The manager wants to choose between immediate advertising and a coverage audit. What should guide the choice?
questions.explanation: The choice between advertising now and a coverage audit rests on whether recorded activity is comparable, because that decides whether the baseline can be trusted. Slide count, adjective count and the order in which the AI lists options are not evidence.

options.label: Which idea fits on fewer slides
The number of adjectives in the draft
Which choice AI mentions first
Whether recorded activity is comparable

questions.prompt: Two alternatives cite the same East total but propose opposite actions. What test is useful?
questions.explanation: When two options start from the same East total but recommend opposite actions, the difference lies in their assumptions. Compare each option's assumptions and the evidence for them. Blending the actions, hiding the conflict or choosing the more confident voice does not resolve it.

options.label: Compare each option's assumptions and evidence
Average the two actions into one plan
Hide the inconsistency from stakeholders
Choose the one with more confident language

questions.prompt: A store-coverage audit is feasible and informs all later options. Why might it come first?
questions.explanation: A coverage audit can show whether East's count is comparable, which reduces uncertainty for every later option. It does not give a profit margin, replace later business evaluation or guarantee growth.

options.label: It establishes a precise profit margin
It reduces uncertainty before intervention
It replaces later business evaluation
It guarantees future regional growth

questions.prompt: AI presents three actions but no evidence required to evaluate them. What is missing?
questions.explanation: An option without the information needed to test it cannot be prioritised or verified. Headings, extra paragraphs about AI or longer lists add volume but not decision logic.

options.label: A more formal heading for each action
An extra paragraph about AI capabilities
A longer list of unrelated activities
Testable information needs for each action

questions.prompt: A team must choose one next investigation. What makes its justification strongest?
questions.explanation: The strongest justification records the trade-off between what you expect to learn and the effort and feasibility of getting it. Promises of success, the AI's ranking or dismissing all other options are claims of authority, not reasons.

options.label: A recorded trade-off between value and feasibility
A promise that the chosen option will succeed
A choice based solely on the AI's ranking
A claim that all other options are useless

questions.prompt: East has the fewest recorded transactions, so the data show that East customers are less interested in buying and a promotion should be the next step.
questions.explanation: False. The count can reflect fewer stores, a shorter reporting window or lower activity, and the CSV cannot separate them. Comparable coverage has to be checked before the count is read as a demand problem or a promotion is chosen.

options.label: True
False

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the Period 11 option process in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Options come first, from the verified diagnosis. Next they are compared in a table so evidence and assumptions are visible. The most attractive one is then challenged, and only after that does a person choose a direction and record the reasoning.

Compare them in a table of evidence, assumption and information needed
Challenge the most attractive option and name alternative explanations
A person chooses a direction and records the justification

questions.prompt: Match each option to the information it needs.
questions.explanation: A coverage check needs the store list, dates and extraction rules. A common-basis comparison needs store IDs, opening days and visits. Acquisition work needs traffic, conversion and campaign costs. A promotion proposal needs two alternative explanations that could be tested before any spending.

pairs.left: Compare activity on a common basis
pairs.right: Store IDs, opening days and customer visits
Traffic or visits, conversion and campaign costs
